name: Tamang, Risiangku dialect
confidence_why: Mazaudon 2014 and 2005, from decades of first-hand work on the Risiangku dialect, explicitly tested and rejected an initial-stress analysis and describe a four-way word-tone system in which all syllables are evenly stressed, Owen-Smith 2015 reports the same word-tone structure and no stress rule for a neighbouring Eastern Tamang dialect, and the only claim of fixed initial word stress, Hari, Taylor and Pike 1970, is about Western Tamang, a different language.

sweep_summary: Eastern Tamang is not in the catalog. The single search hit (Glottolog 48056, Pittman 1971 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies') is the same paper as Pittman 1970 in Hale & Pike, Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal Part II pp. 1-8, already held held by the project (chep1245; copy placed under east2347). Glottolog attached it to taj by 'computerized assignment from \"tamang\"'; the paper's Tamang data are Taylor's Sahugaon material (Western Tamang, tdg) and its 'stressed/unstressed' terms label four tone/register classes of monosyllables, so it is about a different variety and silent on word-stress placement (priority none). this search of works with stress in the title then pulled the open Mazaudon corpus from HAL (2005 proceedings paper, 2014 LD&C article, 2007 French encyclopedia entry, 2008 Phonetica, 1993 orthography paper) plus the held Owen-Smith 2015 SOAS thesis (Indrawati Khola, Sindhupalchok). The best first-hand statement is Mazaudon 2014: 599-600 (with Mazaudon 2005: 10), Risiangku Eastern Tamang: an initial-stress-plus-tone analysis was considered and rejected; suffixes are not weaker in intensity; 'all syllables are evenly stressed'; prosody is four word tones on the phonological word. Reading: no word stress (word-tone language). Unread but potentially relevant: Mazaudon 1973 Phonologie tamang (SELAF, print-only; pp. 61-92 is where the rejection is demonstrated), Poudel 2006 Dhankute Tamang grammar (HathiTrust search-only, Harvard print) and Lee 2011 Eastern Tamang Grammar Sketch (not located) - medium priority as possible modern grammar-based stress remarks. Everything downloaded is with.duckduckgo unreachable, OpenAlex and Google Books APIs not reachable by automated download; HAL needs a non-Mozilla user readers (Anubis challenge). Four small files in the east2347 folder were written there at 10:19 by something other than this readers and were not opened or listed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tamang is a word-tone language: one of four lexical melodies (tone 1-4, distinguished by pitch, phonation and initial voicing) is attached to the root and spread over the entire phonological word (root + suffixes/clitics). There is no culminative word stress: all syllables of the word are evenly stressed, grammatical suffixes are not reduced in intensity, and Mazaudon explicitly rejected an 'initial stress + tone' analysis. Corroborated by Mazaudon 2005 (HAL preprint p. 10): 'Tamang syllables appear to be all about equally stressed'; Bodish languages 'do not generally give prominence, either by way of F0 or intensity, to one syllable per unit'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress at any level within the word per the source).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Tamang. The 2005 paper contrasts Lhasa Tibetan, where inflectional suffixes are de-stressed and tonally extrametrical, with Tamang where they are not. Mazaudon 2007 (encyclopedia preprint) calls grammatical morphemes 'enclitiques et atones', i.e. toneless, not stressless. Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970: 116 claim first-syllable word stress, but for Western Tamang (Sahugaon, Nuwakot), a different language (west2415).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical root plus case/TAM suffixes and enclitics) is the tone domain; the 'first (tonic) syllable' of the word determines the melody (Owen-Smith 2015: 66, citing Mazaudon 1973 ch. 3), but this is tone assignment, not stress. Statements are about connected speech and framed elicitation of Risiangku Tamang.
new_statements.identity_note: All Mazaudon material describes the Risiangku dialect (Sindhupalchok District, east of the Trisuli), which Gao & Mazaudon 2022 (p. 2) label 'Risiangku Tamang, an Eastern Tamang variety (ISO [taj])' = east2347; Owen-Smith 2015 (Indrawati Khola, Sindhupalchok) is the same language. The one source that states a positional stress rule ('always on the first syllable'), Hari, Taylor & Pike 1970: 116, describes the Sahugaon dialect of Nuwakot and calls it 'Western Tamang' = Glottolog west2415 (ISO tdg), a different language; Pittman 1970's 'three-tone, two-stress' remark rests on the same Western data. the copy consulted named mazaudon_2003_tamang_thurgood-lapolla_chapter.* is actually the 2007 French encyclopedia preprint (HAL halshs-00147443), not the Routledge chapter.

new_statements.reading: Eastern Tamang (Risiangku) has no word stress: an initial-stress-plus-tone analysis was explicitly tested and rejected in the primary 1973 phonology, suffix syllables are not weaker in intensity, and all syllables of the word are evenly stressed; prosody is a four-way word-tone contrast anchored on the root and spread over the whole phonological word. If the language is added to the catalog it should be coded as 'no word stress / tone language', not fixed: initial syllable.

new_statements.quote: [p. 292, section 2.6 'Tones'] There are four tones, which apply to phonological words. They are transcribed by a raised number preceding the word. A word can contain several morphemes which are separated by a hyphen in the transcription. The first morpheme determines the tone of the whole word. Particles which carry their own tone are considered separate words, and are not hyphenated with the preceding word. The phonetic pitch of the tones is approximately as follows: 1a, high falling; 2a, mid-high level; 3a, mid-low level; 4a, very low – falling if the word is monosyllabic, falling-rising-falling if the word has two syllables or more. [p. 299, section 5.8] Case markers are all toneless suffixes.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same Risiangku dialect, same analysis type as the catalog record (classification tonal, Mazaudon 2014): a four-way word-tone system anchored on the first morpheme with toneless suffixes. The chapter is silent on stress as such, so it neither repeats nor contradicts the catalog's explicit statement (from Mazaudon 2014: initial-stress-plus-tone analysis rejected, suffixes not weaker); it is fully compatible with 'tone language, no word stress' and gives no support to any fixed-stress coding.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Risiangku (Eastern) Tamang prosody is described purely as word-tone: four tones (two high with clear voice, two low with breathy voice) whose domain is the phonological word; the first morpheme (the root) fixes the tone of the whole word, bound morphemes/case markers are toneless, particles and modals with their own tone count as separate words. The chapter gives no word-stress rule and never uses the words stress or accent; the only other prosodic remark is an emphatic intonation pattern (one syllable of an emphasized word on very high falsetto pitch, p. 294), which is intensification, not lexical stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles carrying their own tone and modals ('fully toned words', p. 302) are separate tonal words; aspiration contrast neutralized under the two low tones (p. 292); emphatic falsetto-pitch intonation on one syllable of an emphasized word (p. 294) is an areal expressive device, not word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter describes the Tamang dialect of Risiangku village, Sindhu Palchok District, Bagmati Zone, 'typical of Eastern Tamang' (p. 291) - the same variety as the catalog entry 'Tamang, Risiangku dialect' (east2347) and as Mazaudon 2014.

readall_conflicts: No new source for east2347 itself was opened, so there is no new disagreement about the Risiangku record. 116; Taylor 1970, p. 243) gives fixed initial word stress plus a stressed/unstressed tone split, but for Western Tamang of Sahugaon, Nuwakot (Glottolog west2415, ISO tdg), a different language from Risiangku Eastern Tamang (east2347, ISO taj). Across the two varieties there is an analytical disagreement: the Pike-school description posits word-initial stress cued by intensity and length, whereas Mazaudon 2014 (existing statement, pp. 599-600) explicitly tested and rejected an 'initial stress with four tones' analysis for Risiangku, finding suffix syllables no weaker and all syllables evenly stressed. That disagreement is partly dialectal and partly a difference of framework and does not bear on the east2347 record, which should stay 'no word stress / word-tone language' as the existing statements say; the catalog's rule field for this item is still empty.

sources.quote: Each phonological word carries one tone, which is determined by the first syllable (the 'tonic syllable'), and is realised across all the syllables of the word (for a detailed account see Mazaudon 1973: chapter 3). Therefore, within the phonological word heterotonic sequences are not attested. The post-tonic syllables of the word have more phonological and phonotactic restrictions than the tonic syllable: they cannot contain long vowels, and can only contain restricted set of consonant clusters.

'Tonic' here means tone-bearing root syllable, not a stress statement; the author says prosody was not investigated. Silent on stress placement.

sources.quote: Le tamang de l'Est, et particulièrement celui du bourg de Risiangku qui sert de référence pour cette présentation, a conservé presque intacte la structure phonologique qu'on peut reconstruire pour l'ensemble de la branche. [...] Les quatre tons du tamang, numérotés de haut en bas de 1 à 4 dans la transcription, sont lexicalement attachés au lexème radical et portent phonologiquement sur le mot entier. Les morphèmes grammaticaux sont enclitiques et atones. [English: Eastern Tamang, particularly that of the village of Risiangku, which serves as reference here, has kept almost intact the phonological structure reconstructible for the whole branch. ... The four Tamang tones, numbered 1-4 from high to low, are lexically attached to the root lexeme and phonologically span the whole word. Grammatical morphemes are enclitic and toneless/unaccented.]

sources.note: HAL abstract read: Tamang-group languages are developing tones from an earlier word-initial voicing opposition (tone split of an old two-tone system: voiceless onsets > 2 high tones, voiced onsets > 2 low tones), with much inter-dialect/inter-speaker variation in the features realising each tone, interpreted as degrees of retention of older features; Risiangku uses F0 and phonation and, less, initial stop voicing as cues to its four tones; the poster examines which old cue Taglung retains (Varenkamp, citing Mazaudon 1978: 169, notes Taglung tone 4 is an extra-high falling tone).
